analysis.one_liner: Lets courts dismiss bankruptcies filed mainly to dodge mass-tort lawsuits and lets victims sue parent companies.
analysis.headline: Referred to the House Judiciary Committee on April 20, 2026, with no action since and just three cosponsors — two Democrats and one Republican.
analysis.plain_summary: Some large companies facing mass lawsuits — over things like asbestos, talc, or opioids — split off a subsidiary, load it with the lawsuits, and file it into bankruptcy, where one judge can cap or wipe out the claims, including claims against the healthy parent company. This bill tells bankruptcy courts they can throw out cases filed mainly for that purpose and, after certain corporate split-ups, lets injured people sue the parent company and its insurers directly instead of being funneled into the bankruptcy. It would apply to cases already open when it takes effect, but it would not undo plans courts have already approved.
analysis.who_benefits: People with injury claims against big companies — for example mass-tort claimants and other creditors — who would no longer have their lawsuits capped or erased by a bankruptcy filed on behalf of a shell subsidiary. Ordinary creditors also gain, because the bill treats a bankruptcy filed only to run out the clock on creditors as grounds for dismissal.

how_it_helps.text: Adds bad-faith and 'objectively futile' filings to the list of reasons a bankruptcy judge must dismiss or convert a Chapter 11 case [S2].
Creates a presumption that a filing is in bad faith when the company manufactured the venue — the practice of shopping for a favorable courthouse [S2].

Creates a conclusive presumption of bad faith when the main purpose of the filing is to cap what the company owes to two or more creditors holding protected claims, when the company went through a divisional merger in the prior four years, or when it has no genuine reorganization purpose [S2].

Carves mass-tort and parent-company claims out of the automatic stay, letting injured people pursue the non-bankrupt parent company, its officers, or its insurers directly after a corporate split-up — including injury claims affecting 100 or more people caused by a product or substance [S2].
Gives creditors' committees a formal voice, requiring courts to weigh their support when deciding whether a case lacks a valid reorganization purpose [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations facing mass-tort liability and their parent companies, which would lose their most powerful tool for capping those lawsuits. Their insurers and the lenders and advisors who structure the split-up transactions also bear costs. Consumers could ultimately see some of these costs passed through.

drawbacks.text: The conclusive bad-faith presumptions are unusually harsh: a company that did a divisional merger for legitimate reasons within the past four years would automatically be presumed to be filing in bad faith, with a heavy burden to prove otherwise [S2].
Applying the rules to cases already in progress could upend deals and timelines in pending cases, adding uncertainty for creditors and claimants alike [S2].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the tradeoff: making bankruptcy harder for companies with huge liabilities could push some into messy state-court litigation or outright liquidation, which can leave injured people with less money overall than a negotiated settlement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people injured by defective products or hazardous substances, the upside is large: today a bankruptcy filed by a shell subsidiary can cap their claims at a fraction of their value, and this bill targets exactly that. The cost falls on the companies and insurers that currently benefit from the tactic. The bill's presumptions are aggressive and could catch some legitimate restructurings, but the core purpose — keeping the bankruptcy system for actual reorganizations rather than liability triage — is a defensible one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on April 20, 2026 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no markup, and no floor vote [S1][S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Emilia Sykes introduced the bill on April 20, 2026, joined by Reps. Lance Gooden and Jerry Nadler, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S2][S4].
It has three cosponsors — two Democrats and one Republican — and no action since the referral [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has changed yet, so the status quo holds: companies that use bankruptcy filings to cap mass-tort liability keep that option, and courts keep handling these questions case by case.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies using bankruptcy to cap lawsuits

sides.party_line_note: No one has opposed it on the record; its sponsorship is bipartisan, with two Democrats and one Republican among three total cosponsors [S3].

industries.industry: Large corporations facing mass-tort liability and their parent companies
industries.note: These companies currently use subsidiary bankruptcies to cap or erase injury claims, including claims against themselves. The bill would let courts dismiss those filings and let victims sue the parent directly [S2].

Insurance-provider claims count as 'protected claims,' so after a qualifying corporate split-up, claimants could pursue the insurer outside the bankruptcy stay instead of having their recovery capped in one proceeding [S2].

industries.industry: Restructuring advisors and lenders who structure corporate split-ups
industries.note: Transactions changing corporate structure within four years of a filing trigger bad-faith presumptions, making these deals riskier to arrange and price. Their business model of engineered bankruptcies loses value, though ordinary restructuring work continues [S2].

industries.industry: Creditors and creditors' committees in Chapter 11 cases
industries.note: Creditors get new grounds to challenge filings that only delay them, and courts must weigh the creditors' committee's position when judging whether a case has a real reorganization purpose [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With only three cosponsors and no committee action since its April 2026 referral, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or floor vote before this Congress ends on January 3, 2027; most bills at this stage die quietly in committee.
